chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Reinforcement Learning for Trading

lessons.title: Where RL Has Actually Worked in Markets: Execution, Market Making, and Position Sizing

body.text: The three places reinforcement learning has genuinely earned a role in trading, order execution, market making, and position sizing, share one trait: each is a narrow, well-defined sequential decision with a measurable cost or reward, not an attempt to predict where the market goes next.

children.text: Optimal Execution: Slicing Big Orders Without Moving the Market

The clearest, most consistently cited application of reinforcement learning in real trading is optimal execution: breaking a large order into smaller pieces and choosing when to release each piece to minimize the total cost of getting filled. A large institutional buy order placed in a single clip visibly moves the price against the buyer, a cost called market impact, so desks instead execute over minutes or hours. The simplest baselines are static schedules: TWAP, time-weighted average price, spreads the order evenly across a time window regardless of what the market is doing, while VWAP, volume-weighted average price, weights the schedule toward periods of historically higher volume. Both ignore what is actually happening in the order book right now.

body.caption: The optimal execution problem framed by Almgren and Chriss (2000): choose an execution trajectory x that balances expected cost, impact from trading too fast, against the variance of that cost, risk from trading too slowly and staying exposed to price drift. An RL agent trained on this objective learns to speed up or slow down execution adaptively instead of following TWAP or VWAP's fixed schedule.

children.text: An RL execution agent takes the same underlying objective and lets the schedule adapt to the state of the order book: current spread, depth at the best few levels, recent volatility, and how much of the order remains to be filled. It can trade faster when the book is deep and liquid, and pull back when a large clip would visibly move the price. This is the closest thing in this course to a settled, production use case for RL: shrinking implementation shortfall on institutional-sized orders, not predicting the market's next move.

children.text: In India, this class of problem sits closest to desks running smart order routing across NSE and BSE, and to firms using NSE's co-location facility to minimize latency on large or time-sensitive orders. It is overwhelmingly an institutional and proprietary trading concern, not something a retail trader placing a handful of lots through a broker API needs to solve, but understanding it explains why optimal execution is the single most credible production RL use case in finance.
Market Making: Managing Inventory While Quoting Two-Sided Prices

A market maker continuously quotes both a bid and an ask, earning the spread between them on round trips while carrying two distinct risks: inventory risk, the danger of accumulating too large a position in one direction if order flow is one-sided, and adverse selection, the risk that whoever is trading against your quote knows something you don't. A market maker who only ever quoted a fixed spread around the last traded price would eventually get run over in one direction and left holding a large, unwanted position.

Avellaneda and Stoikov's 2008 market making model formalizes the fix: instead of quoting symmetrically around the market price, the maker computes a reservation price that skews away from the market price in the direction that reduces current inventory. Carrying a large long position pushes the reservation price down, making the maker more eager to sell and less eager to buy more, nudging inventory back toward flat. An RL agent learning to market make is, in effect, learning a version of this skewing behavior directly from data: state built from current inventory, recent fill rate, and volatility, action built from where to set the bid and ask relative to a reference price, reward built from spread captured net of inventory risk and adverse selection cost.

body.text: Market making of this kind is a licensed, institutional activity on Indian exchanges, run by registered market makers under NSE and BSE schemes, particularly for less liquid options series, and by proprietary trading firms with direct market access. It is not something built casually on a retail brokerage API, but the underlying inventory management logic explains an idea that recurs later in this course: position sizing that responds to what you already hold, not just to the signal in front of you.

children.text: Position Sizing: From the Kelly Criterion to Learned Sizing

The oldest, best-known answer to how much to bet is the Kelly Criterion, published by John Kelly at Bell Labs in 1956 for a completely different problem, noisy telephone lines, before being adopted by gamblers and then traders.

body.caption: Kelly's formula for bet sizing as a fraction of capital: b is the net odds received, p is the probability of winning, and q = 1 - p is the probability of losing. In continuous trading terms this becomes roughly f* ≈ μ / σ², the ratio of expected edge to variance, sizing bets in proportion to how much edge you have and how volatile the outcome is.

children.text: Kelly sizing assumes you already know your edge and its distribution precisely, a static number plugged into a formula. Real trading edges are noisy, time varying, and regime dependent, which is exactly the gap RL-based sizing tries to close: instead of a fixed formula, a trained policy can condition position size on the full state, current confidence in the signal, recent volatility, existing inventory, and learn to size up when conditions favor the strategy and down when they don't, without needing a single static estimate of edge and variance. This does not make it safer by default. An RL sizing policy trained on a reward that ignores risk can just as easily learn to oversize as a human chasing full Kelly without the half-Kelly haircut experienced practitioners use to survive estimation error.

body.title: A Short History Behind Today's RL Trading Tools

events.title: Kelly Criterion Published
events.description: John Kelly Jr. at Bell Labs formalizes optimal bet sizing for maximizing long-run growth, originally for a telecommunications problem.

events.title: Almgren-Chriss Optimal Execution
events.description: Robert Almgren and Neil Chriss publish a framework for optimal execution balancing market impact cost against timing risk, still a reference model execution algorithms are benchmarked against.

events.title: Avellaneda-Stoikov Market Making Model
events.description: Marco Avellaneda and Sasha Stoikov formalize inventory-aware quoting through a reservation price that skews with a market maker's position.

events.title: AlphaGo Beats Lee Sedol
events.description: DeepMind's deep RL system defeats a top Go player, drawing a wave of attention and research funding toward deep reinforcement learning generally, finance included.

events.title: JPMorgan's LOXM Reported
events.description: One of the first large banks to publicly discuss using RL-style learning for equity execution, trained on historical order data rather than a hand-tuned schedule.

events.title: RL in Production Execution and Market Making
events.description: Large global prop trading firms and quant funds run RL-influenced execution and market making systems; RL-based signal generation and standalone strategy design remain far more experimental.

body.text: None of this makes RL sizing a free lunch. A trained policy that maximizes average reward without a variance or drawdown penalty can just as easily learn to oversize as a human chasing full Kelly without the half-Kelly haircut experienced practitioners use to survive estimation error. Chapter 3's reward design lesson exists precisely to stop this from happening by construction, rather than hoping training finds restraint on its own.

body.title: Sizing With and Without State
body.scenario: Two position-sizing approaches are proposed for the same Nifty 50 futures strategy. Approach A uses a fixed fractional rule: always risk 1% of capital per trade, regardless of signal strength or current volatility. Approach B is an RL-learned policy that conditions size on signal confidence, India VIX, and current inventory.
body.prompt: What is the genuine advantage Approach B offers over Approach A, and what new risk does it introduce that Approach A does not have?
body.modelAnswer: Approach B's genuine advantage is that it can size trades in proportion to conviction and market conditions rather than treating every trade identically: a high-confidence signal in a calm, low-volatility regime can be sized up, while a marginal signal in a choppy, high-VIX regime can be sized down or skipped, something a flat 1% rule cannot do. The new risk it introduces is that the sizing behavior itself is now learned rather than fixed, so it depends entirely on the training data, reward function, and validation used to produce it. If the reward function does not explicitly penalize variance or drawdown, or if training data does not include a genuinely stressed regime, Approach B can learn to size up aggressively in exactly the conditions where Approach A's flat, unglamorous 1% rule would have kept losses controlled.

body.title: What Avellaneda-Stoikov Style Skewing Actually Does
body.question: A market maker using inventory-aware quoting has accumulated a large long position because buyers have been more aggressive than sellers all session. What does the reservation price framework predict the maker's quotes should do next?
options: Both bid and ask move up equally, keeping the spread the same width but higher
The reservation price skews down, making the maker relatively more eager to sell and less eager to buy, nudging inventory back toward flat
The maker should stop quoting entirely until inventory returns to zero
Nothing changes; the reservation price only depends on volatility, not inventory
body.explanation: The entire point of an inventory-aware reservation price is that it responds to current position, not just to the market price and volatility. A large long position skews the reservation price down, making the maker's quotes relatively more attractive to sellers and less attractive to buyers, which nudges the position back toward flat without the maker having to stop quoting altogether.

points: Optimal execution, breaking large orders into pieces that adapt to live order book conditions, is the clearest production use case for RL in trading today, closer to cost minimization than market prediction

The Almgren-Chriss framework frames execution as balancing expected market impact cost against the risk of trading too slowly; an RL agent learns to navigate that tradeoff adaptively rather than on a fixed schedule

Market making manages inventory risk by skewing quotes away from a symmetric spread, using something like Avellaneda and Stoikov's reservation price; an RL market maker learns a version of this skewing behavior from data

Execution and market making are overwhelmingly institutional and licensed activities on Indian exchanges, not retail-accessible strategies, but their underlying logic, adapting to live conditions and to your own inventory, recurs throughout this course

The Kelly Criterion gives a classical, formula-based answer to position sizing, but assumes a precisely known, fixed edge; RL-learned sizing tries to condition size on the full state instead, at the cost of depending entirely on training data and reward design
None of these techniques remove the need for risk discipline; a poorly specified reward can teach an RL sizing policy to oversize just as easily as an undisciplined human trader chasing full Kelly
